It is so decided. Mr. President, This year marks the beginning of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea's five-year military development plan for 2026-2030. The DPRK's ninth party congress held from 19 to 25 February noted that under this plan, the DPRK will introduce new secret arsenals and special strategic assets, including the ICBM complexes of ground and underwater launching. Throughout 2025 and into early 2026, the DPRK has continued to conduct ballistic missile launches. This includes short-range ballistic missiles, multiple launch rocket systems, long-range strategic cruise missiles, and anti-ship missiles. In the past month, the DPRK has also tested ballistic missiles equipped with what it calls cluster bomb and fragmentation mine warheads. This month, the Director General of the International Atomic Energy Agency warned of a very serious increase in the DPRK's fissile missile material production capacity at the Yongbyon nuclear site. These developments have been accompanied by statements from the DPRK leader reiterating the country's commitment to further advancing its nuclear and ballistic missile capabilities through qualitative modernization and the diversification of delivery systems. Mr. President, the DPRK's pursuit of nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs in violation of relevant Security Council resolutions remains a matter of serious concern. These activities undermine the global nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation regime, including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. We reiterate our call on the DPRK to fully comply with its international obligations, including the NPT and IAEA safeguards, and to sign and ratify the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty. At this critical juncture, it is essential to underscore the urgent need to reduce nuclear risk, prevent any use of nuclear weapons, and bring about their total elimination. Mr. President, the Security Council last met on this issue in May 2025, one year after the end of the mandate of the panel of experts established pursuant to Resolution 1874. While the panel's mandate was not renewed beyond 30 April 2024, the committee established pursuant to Resolution 1718 continues to oversee the sanctions measures, which remain in place. As the Secretary-General has stated, all countries must abide by the relevant Security Council sanctions in their relations with the DPRK. Mr. President, the broader security landscape on the Korean Peninsula remains tense. with heightened military activities, limited avenues for inter-Korean and regional dialogue, and growing concerns over the potential for miscalculation. The only way to durably reduce tensions and alleviate these concerns is to achieve sustainable peace and the complete and verifiable denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. Dialogue and diplomacy are indispensable to achieving this objective, and we welcome any efforts in this respect. Thank you, Mr. President.
I thank Ms. Di Carlo for her briefing. I now give the floor to Mr. James Byrne.

Mr. President, distinguished members of the Security Council, I appreciate the opportunity to brief you here today. My name is James Burt. I am the CEO and founder of the London-based Open Source Centre, and I'm a senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London. For several years, my team has generated open source evidence on North Korea's illicit trade. Some of this work has focused on the procurement of illicit petroleum. and the export of coal and iron ore conducted in contravention of UN Security Council resolutions. Last year, the Open Source Center presented evidence to the council of six vessels loading prohibited cargo within North Korean territory, establishing a clear pattern of activity in violation of these resolutions. These resolutions, including 2371 and 2397, specifically prohibit any type of transfer and export of North Korean coal and iron ore. They also state the revenues generated from the exports of coal and other commodities directly contribute to the DPRK's nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles programs. What we will show you here today is clear evidence that this pattern persists. evidence supported by a methodology that integrates high resolution satellite imagery, AIS transponder records and vessel specification databases. This approach allows for the definitive identification of vessels loading coal and other commodities in contravention of these UN Security Council resolutions. From November 2025 to April 2026, the Open Source Center has observed at least five additional vessels conducting eight journeys into North Korea to load cargo such as coal and iron ore. As can be seen in this overview slide, these are the Orion, the Peaceful Eight, the Ostrov and Siferova, the Dream Wave, and the Furunda One. Three of these vessels were recently deflagged by their respective flag states. Two, the Orion and the Ostrov Antiferova continue to sail under a Russian flag. One, the Dreamwave was recently flagged to Tanzania. The evidentiary standard for inclusion today is high. we have not included a number of additional vessels that we believe have likely visited to load coal and other commodities. The first case and the most recent of these vessels is a 130 meter long cargo ship named Orion, loading coal at the North Korean port of Songnim in mid-April, 2026. The Orion started its journey in Sakhalin, Russia, on 6 April. From here, it sailed around the Korean peninsula and through the Yellow Sea. AIS data from the ship's transponder showed the vessel was transmitting inside North Korean territorial waters and the port of Songnim on 16, 18 and 20 April. Over this period, we collected imagery of different kinds from three different commercial providers, Satellogic, Umbra, and Vantel, using different kinds of satellite sensors. These sensors independently show the same thing, the Orion loading coal in North Korea. These images, are available for anyone that cares to subscribe to these services and clearly show the vessel at the location where the ship's transponder was openly transmitting on 18 April at 8:36 UTC. These images also clearly show large piles of coal at the loading berths next to the Orion. In particular, an image on 19 April clearly shows coal being loaded into the hold of the vessel, which has its cargo hatches open. The images show the coal piles decreasing in size over time, in addition to trucks and excavators moving coal towards the feeder belts, which are being used to load the Orion. It's very clear in this image. The Orion is the latest instance of a foreign flag vessel sailing into North Korea to load these commodities. However, since November 2025, the Open Source Center has identified an additional four vessels also loading commodities such as coal and iron ore in North Korea. In our last presentation to the Security Council in May 2025, we detailed some of the deceptive shipping practices that these vessels undertook to disguise their activities. These practices have continued, but in recent months we have seen increasingly complex and coordinated scheme designed to disguise these activities. In one such instance, as you can see here, a 130 meter long vessel named the Peaceful Eight, also known as the Runder Eight, spoofed an extended trip into the Russian Far East in order to disguise its illicit activities in Vonsan. in North Korea on 17, 19 and 20 March. Although the vessel was transmitting its position as sailing towards Russian waters, satellite imagery shows there was no vessel at these locations. As you can see here in this image taken by Planet Labs, what do you see over those coordinates? Open ocean. There is no vessel there. Instead, high resolution images taken by Planet Labs, taken by high resolution images taken on the same day show that the vessel was in one sun. And as you can see here, loading coal. As in the case of the Orion, in these images, we can see the cargo hatches are open and coal is being loaded into the hold. But there are other vessels as well. This is the Ostrov Ansiferova. In February, March and April 2026, a 97 meter long cargo vessel named Ostrov Ansiferova was observed across three separate trips to the North Korean port of Chongjin. On the first trip, on 13 and 15 February, the vessel was observed with its cargo bays open at the coal terminal. On 15 February, In this image, coal piles were observed next to the vessel with its cargo hold open again with cranes on the pier in use. On the second trip on 12 and 13 March, the vessel was observed back in Chongjin again with its cargo hold open next to piles of commodities on the pier. And there is a third trip as well. This on the third, you can see the vessel was observed again on 10 April back in Chongjin, once again berthed with its cargo hold open. This is the Dream Wave. In November 2025, the Dream Wave, a 99 meter long vessel, was anchored outside the port of Tancheon, North Korea. Subsequent imagery shows the vessel sailing into port towards coal stored on the pier. And this is can be seen in these two images that we have here today. One last vessel we are going to present on is the Furundar 1. This on the other side of the country in February 2026, the Furunda one was observed leaving the North Korean port of Nampo after birthing at the coal terminal. In these two images we have here today, you can clearly see it in the port and then you can clearly see it leaving with cargo coal in the hold and its cargo hatch open. Mr. President, taken together, this evidence confirms that at least five cargo vessels, the Orion, the Peaceful Eight, the Ostrov Amziferova, the Dream Wave, and the Furunda One have continued to load sanctioned commodities in North Korean ports for delivery abroad. This is not a series of isolated incidents. It is an ongoing pattern of UN sanctions violations. Several of these vessels have visited repeatedly. and these presented here today is not an exhaustive list. This evidence we will publish later on the Open Source Centre's website. This methodology that we use to identify these vessels integrates commercial high resolution satellite imagery, transponder logs, vessel databases and a range of other open sources. It is consistent with the rigorous standards established by the UN panel of experts. These findings represent a factual record of ongoing violations that directly fund North Korea's prohibited weapons program. We submit this record to the Council and we remain at your service and disposable for further inquiry. Thank you, Mr. President, for your time.
I thank Mr. Byrne for his briefing. I now give the floor to those Council members who wish to make a statement. I give the floor to the representative of United States.

Thank you, Mr. President. I want to thank Under Secretary General DiCarlo and Mr. Byrne for their briefings today. Colleagues, nearly two years ago, a Russian veto eliminated the 1718 committee panel of experts with China standing silently by robbing this Council and UN member states of independent credible reporting on sanctions violations Russia did this for one key reason to hide its own violations from scrutiny The United States is grateful to independent experts like the Open Source Center for stepping into the breach and keeping the spotlight on UN sanction evasions and violations. Mr. Byrne briefed the work of his team to us on May 2025, and he is back today because these violations continue. The information presented to us today is not speculative. The evidence is irrefutable. Vessels are loading DPRK origin coal and iron ore at North Korean ports and sailing to destinations, most notably to China, in direct violation of this council's resolutions. Let me be crystal clear about what this means. In 2017, this council passed resolution 2371 explicitly prohibiting the export of DPRK coal iron and iron ore. The revenue from these exports directly fund North Korea's unlawful nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs. Every ton of coal loaded onto these vessels, every shipment that reaches a foreign port, every dollar or yuan that flows back to Pyongyang brings the DPRK one step closer to threatening the world with nuclear catastrophe. This is not an abstract concern. This is one of the gravest threats to international peace and security today. The Open Source Center's findings confirm what the United States has been tracking for months. We have identified these vessels. We know their routes. We know their operators. And we will not stand by while they operate with impunity. In December 2025, the United States nominated seven vessels for designation in the 1718 Committee. Those seven nominations are still under review months later, despite being supported by the same irrefutable evidence that we saw here today. This briefing shows additional vessels now engaged in the same prohibited activity. In the coming days, the United States will nominate the vessels identified in today's briefing for designation in the 1718 Committee. We call on the Committee to act without delay to designate all of the vessels involved in these smuggling operations, including those we nominated months ago. The 1718 Committee has a mandate. to oversee the implementation of UN Security Council sanctions on the DPRK, including by designating violators. This is not optional. This is the committee's responsibility. UN sanctions exist as a peaceful lever for addressing threats to international peace and security. They are the alternative to military action. The evidence presented today leaves no room for doubt, and it is drawn from readily available commercial satellite imagery and standard vessel tracking software accessible to anyone. If some members of this Council choose to ignore these violations, they are making a deliberate choice to enable the DPRK's nuclear weapons program. The United States will not make that choice. We will continue to identify violators, nominate them for designation, and work with our partners to ensure that they face consequences, whether through this council or through other means. Mr. President, the DPRK's unlawful nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs are a threat to the Korean Peninsula, the Indo-Pacific, and to the entire world. This Council was created to address exactly these kinds of threats. It's time we did our actual jobs. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United States for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of Denmark.

Thank you, Mr. President. And let me also thank Under-Secretary-General Di Carlo and Mr. Byrne for their briefings. In the unfortunate absence of a panel of experts, these presentations are highly valuable. As we've heard, the DPRK's continued unacceptable and illegal behavior clearly constitutes a threat, not only to regional peace and security on the Korean Peninsula, but globally. Mr. President, just this week in the General Assembly Hall, the state parties to the Treaty on Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons are meeting for the review conference. Sadly, in the midst of this strong push to protect the world from the curse of nuclear war, the DPRK continues its quest for nuclear weapons. Earlier this month, the IAEA's Director General concluded that the DPRK has made a very serious increase in its capabilities to produce nuclear weapons. The IAEA also documented a worrying expansion of the Yongbyon Nuclear Scientific Research Center, including a suspected new uranium enrichment facility. Just this year, we've also witnessed six ballistic missile launches, three of which took place this month. So let us face the facts. The DPRK is evidently and brazenly continuing to develop both its nuclear program and its ballistic missile programs. These acts are not only ongoing, they're escalating. That is why Denmark jointly called for this meeting to shine a light on these deeply concerning developments. Mr. President, the DPRK and all UN member states without exception must abide by the resolutions of this Council. Denmark is deeply worried by the illegal military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. The DPRK's armed deliveries and troop deployments in support of Russia's illegal war in Ukraine are dangerous and escalatory. In return, Russia provides military support, including missile-related technology, to the DPRK. Such actions flagrantly violate Security Council resolutions, including the two-way arms embargo. This is a prime example of how the DPRK's actions do not just concern the countries of its region, but gravely impact peace and security across the globe. The sanctions against the DPRK remain fully in effect. However, implementation oversight has been severely over hampered for the past two years following Russia's veto of the extension of the mandate of the panel of experts. As a result, it has become easier for the DPRK and others to violate and circumvent sanctions. Mr. President, Denmark supports the use of sanctions against the DPRK as a legitimate tool to pressure the regime to end its illegal actions. In a world already torn by conflict and insecurity, we cannot allow such reckless behaviour to continue. At the same time, we recall that sanctions are not intended to negatively impact the lives of civilians. To this end, We support the swift approval of all legitimate humanitarian exemption requests in accordance with applicable sanctions. We remain deeply concerned about the dire humanitarian and human rights situation in the DPRK. We call on the DPRK to start prioritizing the well-being of its citizens over its dangerous weapons programs. We also urge the DPRK to allow the return of the UN and humanitarian organizations into the country and to engage seriously with the UN human rights mechanisms. In closing, we welcome all efforts to build positive momentum into inter-Korean relationship. The Republic of Korea has publicly announced that it stands ready to resume dialogue. We strongly encourage the DPRK to do the same. to engage constructively and to return to dialogue. Denmark fully supports all efforts towards the denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. To reach this goal, the DPRK must abide by its international obligations. This means returning to compliance with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and abandoning its ballistic missiles program and its existing nuclear programs in a complete, verifiable and irreversible manner. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Denmark for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of France.

Thank you, Mr. President. I wish first and foremost to thank the Under Secretary General for Political Affairs, Madam Rosemary DiCarlo, as well as Mr. James Byrne, Chief Executive Officer and Founder of Open Source Center. Their briefings serve as a reminder of the need for the Security Council to keep its attention focused on the North Korean proliferation crisis and to see to it that its resolutions are implemented. For this reason, France joined five other members of the Security Council in calling requesting the conduct of this meeting, including South Korea and Japan, as they requested in the 24 April last letter. Mr. President, since Monday, the 11th Conference on Non-Proliferation was held, and this is a virtually universal treaty which represents the cornerstone of the international non-proliferation disarmament regime, and now more than ever before this needs to be preserved and upheld by Addressing during addressing the review conference, the debate, the Foreign Minister of France, Mr. Abbaro, recalled that one of the major threats to this regime. the non-proliferation regime and the threats to international security remained, the ongoing pursuit by North Korea of its nuclear and ballistic programs, illegal nuclear ballistic programs for the past 20 years, flouting its international obligations, including the resolutions unanimously adopted by the Security Council, North Korea conducted six nuclear tests. It continued to develop nuclear weapons and has enshrined this in its constitution, It has engaged in fine tuning ballistic capabilities since 2022, for example, engaging in more than 100 missile, uh, test strikes of various… ranges. These violations undermine the authority of Security Council resolutions. They undermine the non-proliferation regime, and it is in our interest, our common interest, to uphold this. They constitute a threat to regional stability and the security of neighboring states. France reaffirms our solidarity with South Korea and with Japan in the face of these North Korean provocations. Our President to recall the solidarity during his visit to those two countries early in the month of April. On that occasion, France extended our support for the efforts of South Korea as they seek to rekindle inter-Korean dialogue and to build confidence-building measures and measures for de-escalation. And we regret the fact that Pyongyang failed to reciprocate in this willingness to engage in dialogue by initiating further ballistic missile tests five during the month of April alone. We remain concerned, Mr. President, by the fact that a permanent member of the Security Council continues to provide its protection and even is complicit in North Korean violations of the resolutions which this permanent member supported. The Russian Federation and North Korea have been engaging in illicit nuclear cooperation, which has included arms transfers between the two countries and the deployment of North Korean soldiers on the Ukrainian front. This North Korean support for the war of aggression against Ukraine is a violation of the UN Charter and a violation of Security Council resolutions. This cooperation remains close. There have been recent visits of Russian senior officials, which are a reflection of this. To avoid accountability, Russia alone cast a veto on the extension of the POE mandate, whose mandate concluded exactly two years ago. The non-renewal of the panel of experts is a significant obstacle to the work of the committee and obstructs the right of all member states to have independent impartial information about implementation of security council resolutions. Amid these dangerous circumstances, Mr. President, we need to continue to remain mobilized to ensure implementation of Security Council resolutions and the attainment of the goals set out thereunder. We reiterate our messages consistently, including during the work of the NPT Review Conference, and we hope to be able to take that opportunity to bring together a large number of supporters for the declaration on North Korean nuclear challenge prepared jointly with South Korea. First and foremost, France calls upon the Security Council to resume work with a view to reconstituting the panel of experts whose work is of critical importance in providing support for the 1718 committee and the implementation of its mandate. And in order to provide information to member states pending a restoration and reconstitution of the panel, France will continue to -- with 10 partners, including South Korea and Japan, to contribute to a monitoring team to produce reports on violations of the sanctions regime related to North Korea. If -- this is not a substitute for the panel of experts, but the initiative helps to bridge the gaps thereunder in this initiative is in accordance with Security Council resolutions. Paragraph 41 of Resolution 2270 explicitly calls upon member states to share all information in their possession about noncompliance with resolutions relating to North Korea. Next, we encourage the committee to continue its efforts to ensure effective implementation of Security Council resolutions. France stands ready in this regard to consider the proposal of the United States to designate seven vessels that were identified in sanctions violations. North Korea, lastly, we call upon North Korea to revert back to compliance with its international obligations, to engage in the path towards diplomacy and to conduct discussions with a view to complete verifiable and irreversible denuclearization. Thank you.
I thank the representative of France for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of Latvia.

Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank Under-Secretary-General Di Carlo for her briefing and Mr. Byrne for his useful contribution in providing the council with facts. Let me reiterate the council's strong condemnation of the DPRK's nuclear and ballistic weapon programmes, which violate multiple Security Council resolutions. We express our regret that it has been two years since the 1718 committee has been unable to function properly, due to the disbandment of its panel of experts. The veto used by Russia was an example of its deliberate efforts to undermine the work of this Council. It was also an early precedent of backing regimes that are willing to support its own brutal aggression against Ukraine, even if it means obstructing the work of this Council and its subsidiary organs. The absence of a panel of experts for the 1718 committee effectively means that the most thorough of UN Security Council sanction tools has been weakened through a lack of access to vital information. Fortunately, due to the joint efforts of states who have contributed to establishment of the multilateral sanctions monitoring team, the international community continues to receive verified and reliable information that helps to bridge the present information gap. Mr. President, it is critically important to remain informed about the situation surrounding the DPRK sanctions, especially considering the various efforts by the DPRK to evade and circumvent them. The state remains one of the main threats to international peace and security. The DPRK continues to develop its illegal nuclear ballistic missile programmes, growing its illegal arsenal and testing new weapon systems. including cluster munitions, as recently reported. And we affirm our robust commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the Korean peninsula. In this regard, we appreciate the efforts made by the Republic of Korea to advance dialogue, and we call on the DPRK to reciprocate in good faith and to comply with its obligations under international law. The DPRK has also provided significant support to the aggressor Russia, both in armaments, from munitions to missiles, as well as in manpower, with thousands of North Korean soldiers deployed in support of Russia's imperial ambitions. This unlawful cooperation must cease, and the DPRK must bear full accountability for its participation in this. Mr. President, We must emphasise another illicit practice in common between Russia and the DPRK, which is the use of old and unsafe vessels flying a flag of a different nationality altogether, the shadow fleet, to evade sanctions. As expressed by many delegations earlier this week in the open debate on maritime security, shadow fleet vessels risk ecological disasters wherever they go, with no accountability. The DPRK is using such vessels to circumvent the sanctions imposed by this Council, using fraudulent documentation, masking movements of ships, engaging in illicit ship-to-ship transfers in order to finance its illegal weapons programme. This is unacceptable, and we must be resolute in upholding this Council's binding decisions. Latvia supports the listing of seven vessels for violating the DPRK sanctions regime as proposed by the United States in late 2025, and we are open to consider additional listings if necessary. Finally, we reiterate the urgent need to re-establish the panel of experts of the 1718 Committee for this Council and the Committee to carry out their full mandates. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Latvia for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of United Kingdom.

Thank you, President, and thank you, Under Secretary-General De Carlo and Mr. Byrne, for your evidence-based and detailed briefings. It was a calculated move to obscure the DPRK's unlawful pursuit of weapons of mass destruction and to conceal Russia's own systematic erosion of the UN sanctions architecture, which, as with all UN member states, it is duty bound to uphold. Without the panel, we have been deprived of crucial Security Council resolution violation monitoring, analysis, and oversight. In vetoing the panel, Russia also cleared a path to expand its military relationship with the DPRK. Pyongyang has supplied more than 11,000 troops to Russia's illegal war against Ukraine, along with munitions and missiles. In return, the DPRK has enjoyed Russia's patronage, provision of critical goods through arms for oil exchanges, and gained increased technical and military capabilities from its combat experience. Russia has also recklessly called DPRK's denuclearization a closed issue. we reaffirm our full commitment to non-proliferation obligations. At this year's NPT Review Conference, we are calling on all UN members to encourage the DPRK to dismantle its nuclear and ballistic missile programs, to reengage in meaningful dialogue, and to return to full NPT compliance. Thank you. I thank the representative of the United Kingdom for the statement. I give the floor to the representative of Panama.

Thank you, President. Madam Chair, I was grateful for the convening of this briefing and for the briefings provided by Ms. Rosemary DiCarlo, Under Secretary General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, and by Mr. James Byrne of the Open Source Center. Both briefings confirm that this file continues to demand technical rigor and political consistency. We also recognize the efforts made by the Republic of Korea to keep channels of communication open, to build bridges, and to provide an environment that is more conducive to dialogue. At an international time marked by polarization and mistrust, any initiative aimed at reducing tensions warrants our support. President, Panama notes with concern that, according to the most recent public findings of the International Atomic Energy Agency, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea continues to develop its nuclear program. The most recent report points to activities that attest to the expansion of enrichment capabilities, the continued operation of sensitive facilities, and other disturbing developments. At the same time, the agency continues not to have access inside the country to carry out independent verification work. This reality should lead us to a simple conclusion. When there is no transparency, uncertainty increases. When there is no verification, mistrust grows. And when mistrust grows, the space for diplomatic solutions shrinks. For this reason, Panama calls on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea to return in good faith to the negotiating table. At the same time, we urge it to resume its engagement with the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and to fully cooperate with the International Atomic Energy Agency. The populations on the Korean peninsula deserve to have real prospects of peace, stability and the certainty for lasting security. This call is all the more relevant since the 11th review conference of the parties to the treaty on the non-proliferation of nuclear weapons is currently being held in New York. In this context, any step towards renewing engagement with multilateral frameworks for trust, accountability and international oversight would be welcomed by the international community. We must also be clear on another fundamental aspect. No unilateral declaration can alter the legal realities established by international law or by the relevant resolutions of this Council. The decisions of this body are legally binding and must be implemented consistently, seriously and non-selectively. Panama further believes that the loss of technical monitoring and reporting capacity following the dissolution of the 1718 Committee Panel of Experts in March 2024 has eroded collective trust. The effective implementation of any regime of measures requires credible supervision, objective data, and reliable technical mechanisms. In the absence of a mechanism keeping this Council constantly updated, it is increasingly difficult to assess the development of the situation on the ground. Reactivating the panel of experts would serve not only the objective of non-proliferation but also any future diplomatic process. The measures taken by this Council should coexist alongside effective humanitarian access with safeguards that avoid imposing unnecessary suffering on the population. Panama is convinced that acting firmly and with resolve and promoting dialogue and diplomacy are not mutually exclusive. They are, on the contrary, essential preconditions to reach a sustainable and peaceful solution. Thank you very much.
